newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FOCUS-Philippines shields economy from Thai woes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Philippines shields economy from Thai woes.

text.p: The Philippines, terrified it would be dragged down by Thailand's baht devaluation, sold hundreds of millions of dollars and forced up interest rates to shield its own currency.
"We have to do something (to defend the peso)," Central Bank Governor Gabriel Singson told Reuters after Thailand effectively devalued its currency on Wednesday morning.

Since April, the Philippines has had to repeatedly defend itself from speculative attacks on its currency and stock market as investors gambled that it would be tripped up by successive economic catastrophes in neighbouring Thailand.
The Philippine peso struggled to hold up in the face of the latest attack only with the help of heavy dollar selling by the Central Bank and sharply higher interest rates.
It increased its one-day reverse repurchase rate twice during the morning to 24 percent, up from 15 percent when the paper was last offered three weeks ago.
The rate usually serves as a benchmark for the closely-wtached Central Bank overnight interest rate a day later.
Trading in the Manila peso market surged to more than 800 million dollars in the morning, its highest on record.
Traders estimated that more than half of the amount was in Central Bank dollar sales.
By midday the peso was quoted at 26.379 to the dollar, little changed from the previous close.
Concerns over the peso also battered the foreign-dominated Philippine stock market which tumbled almost two percent.
"You should expect some initial spillover effect. I am very confident this will settle down," the Central Bank's Singson said.
But he warned that the Bank would take any measures it thought necessary to beat off speculators and to keep the peso stable, which is the central plank of its monetary policy.
"We are determined to defend out currency," Singson said.

"We have shown our determination in the past to defend the currency from speculative attacks. This is a speculative attack on the currency resulting from what happened in Thailand...it is not affecting the fundamentals. The fundamentals are still good."

But bankers warned that persistently high interest rates to defend the peso -- whose stability the Central Bank considers crucial to keep inflation under control -- could in the end cost the economy dear.
"It might be too expensive in the long-term. Something's got to give," Banco Santander Treasurer Antonio Agcaoili said.

There have already been signs that the country's manufacturing industry is not doing quite as well as had been hoped and many economists doubt the economy will reach the government's target for this year of seven pecent growth.
Exporters have also been pleading with the government to let the peso fall to make their products more competitive in overseas markets.
